title: How Volcanoes Work
subject: Geography
text: Deep beneath our feet, the Earth is extremely hot. In some places the rock gets so hot that it melts. This melted rock is called magma. Because magma is lighter than the solid rock around it, it slowly rises upwards, collecting in large underground pools called magma chambers.

When the pressure in a magma chamber becomes too great, the magma forces its way up through cracks in the Earth's crust. When it bursts out at the surface, we call it an eruption. Once magma reaches the surface, it gets a new name: lava.

Not all volcanoes erupt in the same way. Some, like those in Hawaii, release runny lava that flows gently down their slopes. Others, like Mount Vesuvius in Italy, explode violently, throwing ash and rocks high into the sky. In the year 79, an eruption of Vesuvius buried the Roman town of Pompeii under several metres of ash.

Volcanoes that have erupted recently and could erupt again are called active. Those that have not erupted for a very long time but might one day are called dormant, which means 'sleeping'. Volcanoes that scientists believe will never erupt again are called extinct.

exercises.question: What is melted rock called while it is still underground?
exercises.explanation: It is called magma underground and lava once it reaches the surface.

exercises.question: Why does magma rise upwards?
options: Because it is lighter than the solid rock around it
Because it is colder than the rock around it
exercises.answer: Because it is lighter than the solid rock around it
